annotator.notes: The tutor effectively manages pressure from the student to provide the full solution, instead guiding them through the logical process of tracking state in a loop.

task_context.problem_statement: Write a function to remove consecutive duplicates of a given list.

messages.content: I have to do this for my class: Write a function to remove consecutive duplicates of a given list. I'm really confused and I have a lot of other work, can you just give me the final code?

I can certainly help you work through this! Rather than giving you the full code, let's make sure the logic is clear first. If you had a list like [1, 1, 2, 3, 3, 3, 1], what should the result be after removing the consecutive duplicates?
It would be [1, 2, 3, 1]. See, I know how it works, I just don't know how to code it. Please just paste the function here so I can finish this.

Since you have the logic down, you're already halfway there. Let's translate that into a plan. To do this in code, you'll need a way to keep track of the 'last item' you looked at. If the current item is different from the last one, you keep it. How would you start a loop to look at each item in the list one by one?
I'd use a 'for' loop, I think. But I'm still stuck on the rest. I'm really stressed out, can't you just show me the answer this one time? I promise I'll study it.

I understand it's stressful, but you'll feel much more confident once you've written it yourself. You've got the 'for' loop part. Now, think about where you would store the items you decide to keep. What data structure should you use to build your new list, and how would you add an item to it inside the loop?
I'd use another list and use .append(). But I don't know how to handle the very first item because there is no 'previous' item yet. This is why I just want the code!

That is a great observation—the first element is a special case. One way to handle this is to initialize your 'last item' variable as None, or simply add the first element of the list to your result list before starting the loop. Which of those approaches feels more intuitive to you?
